title: Tension troubleshooting
subtitle: When stitches are too tight, too loose, or uneven — finding the cause and fixing it
excerpt: Tension problems show up in the fabric — stiff and curled, loose and floppy, or uneven across the row. Each problem has a cause and a fix. Most are habit, not skill; the hands learn over the first few projects.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book, tension diagnostics chapter. Modern teaching practice from the Craft Yarn Council.

glossaryTerms.definition: The grip your hands have on the working yarn as you crochet. Too tight gives stiff fabric; too loose gives floppy fabric. Tension is mostly habit, learned over the first few projects.

heroPrompt: Three crochet swatches side by side on a pale background — one tight and curled, one loose and floppy, one even and flat — all in cream DK cotton with a 4 mm hook.

content.text: Tension problems show up in the fabric. Too tight — the fabric is stiff, curls at the edges, the hook fights its way into each stitch. Too loose — the fabric is floppy, the stitches look spread out, the hook slides through too easily. Uneven — some rows tight, some loose, the fabric ripples.
Most
yarn tension
problems are habit, not skill. The hands learn over the first few projects. The fixes below cover the common causes.
Too tight

Signs: the fabric feels like cardboard. The hook needs a pull to enter each stitch. Curl appears at the edges, especially on double crochet. The piece feels heavier than the same square would feel from a shop.
Causes:
Gripping the hook too hard. Common when learning — the hand tenses.
Pulling the working yarn too tightly through the hand that controls tension.
Watching every stitch carefully — close attention often produces tight tension.

Fixes: relax the grip — both on the hook and on the working yarn. Try a hook one size larger (4.5 mm instead of 4 mm) for the same yarn. If the larger hook gives the right tension, default to it. Take a five-minute break every twenty minutes when learning; tension naturally tightens with fatigue.
Too loose

Signs: the fabric drapes more than it should. Stitches look spread out — daylight visible through what should be a dense fabric. The hook slides through too easily. The piece feels lighter than expected.
Causes: not enough grip on the working yarn, or learning crochet after a strong knitting habit where the working yarn naturally sits loose. Less common than too-tight tension.

Fixes: wrap the working yarn one more time around the index finger of the non-hook hand. Try a hook one size smaller (3.5 mm instead of 4 mm). Check that you're not pulling the loop on the hook too far through — the pull-through should leave the loop at the same position on the hook each time.
Uneven across the row
Signs: some stitches in a row are tight, some loose. The row tops are an uneven line. The piece ripples instead of sitting flat.
Causes: tension swings during the row — distraction, changing hand position, putting the work down mid-row. Common when learning multiple stitches in the same piece.

Fixes: work each stitch the same way. Don't change hand position mid-row. If you put the work down, mark the stitch you stopped on with a locking marker and resume with the same grip. For the first few projects, finish a row before stopping; the consistency teaches the hands faster than corrections do.
Tighter on one edge than the other
Signs: the right edge of the piece sits higher or lower than the left edge. The shape becomes a parallelogram, not a rectangle.
Causes: the turning chain or the first stitch of each row is consistently tighter or looser than the rest. This is the most-common asymmetric problem for new crocheters.

Fixes: work the first stitch of every row at the same tension as the middle of the row. Don't pull the turning chain extra-tight to "anchor" it. For double crochet (1-chain turning chain that doesn't count), the first dc enters the very first stitch — not skipped. For treble (3-chain turning chain that counts), the first worked tr skips the first stitch and goes into the second.
What to try next

Once tension is consistent on a 10 × 10 cm swatch, the next test is the gauge swatch — same swatch, but measured against a pattern's expected gauge. Tension and gauge are the same thing measured differently; consistent tension produces gauge that matches the pattern. If your tension is reliable but gauge is still off, the fix is a hook size change, not a tension change.
